subject: typescript
title: Generics
description: Type parameters, inference from arguments, constraints with extends, and default type arguments.

content.title: Definition
content.body: A generic is a type parameter: a placeholder the caller fills in. It lets one function or type keep an exact relationship between its input and its output instead of falling back to any.

content.title: Inference from the call site
content.body: You rarely pass type arguments by hand — TypeScript reads them off the arguments.

content.title: Good practice
content.body: Constrain a type parameter when you need to read from it: <T extends { id: string }> lets you touch .id while keeping the caller's exact type in the return.

exercises.question: What is the inferred type of x?
exercises.explanation: T is inferred as number from the argument, so items[0] is number.

exercises.question: Complete the constraint so the body may read entity.id.
exercises.explanation: extends constrains the type parameter. Without it, T could be anything and .id would not be known to exist.

exercises.question: What does a generic give you that any does not?

answers.text: It preserves the relationship between argument and return type, so the caller keeps full type information
It allows more value types to be passed in
It makes the function faster at runtime

exercises.explanation: any accepts everything and returns everything, losing the link. A type parameter carries the caller's type all the way through.

exercises.question: Which line does the compiler reject?

answers.text: Line 4 — the type argument must be passed explicitly
Line 1 — a generic needs a default type argument
Line 2 — length does not exist on an unconstrained T

exercises.explanation: T is unknown inside the body until it is constrained. <T extends { length: number }> makes line 2 legal.

exercises.question: Generics are erased at compile time and add no runtime code.
exercises.explanation: Like every other type in TypeScript, a type parameter disappears in the emitted JavaScript.

exercises.question: What is the type of result?
exercises.explanation: T is string[], so b.value is an array and .length is a number.

exercises.question: Complete the declaration so Box defaults to holding a string.
exercises.explanation: A default type argument uses =. It can be combined with a constraint: <T extends object = {}>.

exercises.question: TypeScript · generics
exercises.front: function get<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K]
exercises.back: A typed property getter — the return type follows the key that was passed
exercises.explanation: This is the canonical generic pair: K is constrained to the object's own keys, and T[K] is an indexed access type.

exercises.topic: When not to use a generic
exercises.question: A type parameter appears exactly once, in one parameter position, and nowhere in the return type. What does that suggest?

answers.text: It should be given a default type argument
It should be constrained more tightly
The generic is not earning anything — the constraint itself would do
Nothing — this is the normal shape of a generic

exercises.explanation: A type parameter relates two positions. Used once, it adds noise: take the constraint as the parameter type directly.

exercises.question: What is the type of result?
exercises.explanation: T comes from the array, U from the callback's return type. Two parameters inferred from two positions is exactly what generics are for.

exercises.question: What does `T extends string ? A : B` mean in a type position?

answers.text: A conditional type: resolves to A when T is assignable to string, otherwise B
A constraint requiring T to be a string
A runtime check compiled into the output
A declaration that T inherits from string

exercises.explanation: It is a type-level if. Over a union it distributes member by member, which is how Exclude and NonNullable are built.

exercises.question: Complete the conditional type that pulls the element type out of an array.
exercises.code: type ElementOf<T> = T extends (___ U)[] ? U : never;
exercises.explanation: infer introduces a type variable inside the condition and binds it to whatever matched. ReturnType and Awaited are written the same way.

exercises.question: Passing a type argument explicitly, as in first<string>(items), disables inference for that call.
exercises.explanation: It also disables the error you would otherwise get from a mismatch, so it is worth a second look in review when the argument could have been inferred.

exercises.question: Why does line 2 fail to compile?

answers.text: T is the caller's exact type, and the extra property makes the result not assignable to it

exercises.explanation: Returning T is a promise to give back exactly the caller's type. Declare the return as T & { mergedAt: number } instead.

exercises.question: What does `<T extends object = Record<string, unknown>>` declare?

answers.text: A parameter constrained to object types, defaulting to a string-keyed record when omitted
A parameter that must be exactly Record<string, unknown>
A syntax error — a constraint and a default cannot be combined
A parameter whose default is checked at runtime

exercises.explanation: Constraint and default are independent, and the default must itself satisfy the constraint.
